segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Some kids are at a rest stop parking lot in the middle of August, waiting to get back in the car-- Logan, William, and Kieran. A reporter approaches them.

segments.speaker: Reporter
segments.text: I couldn't help but notice that there's three of you guys. So the first question that pops into my head is, who's going to have to ride in the middle?

segments.speaker: Boy
segments.text: Unfortunately, me.

segments.speaker: Reporter
segments.text: And how come you're the guy who has to ride in--

segments.speaker: Boy
segments.text: Because those two, um, basically-- I don't know. They fight when they're in the middle. He doesn't even want to sit next to him. Ow. Stop that!

segments.speaker: Reporter
segments.text: He's pinching your cheek right now.

segments.speaker: Boy
segments.text: Pressure pointing, actually.

segments.speaker: Reporter
segments.text: So do you feel like this is going to be-- this is always going to be your job? As you guys get older, you're always going to be the brother sitting in the middle, brokering the peace?

segments.speaker: Boy
segments.text: Yeah. And basically, I'm the mediator.

segments.speaker: Reporter
segments.text: How do you mean?

segments.speaker: Boy
segments.text: I'm not sure what you're talking about.

segments.speaker: Reporter
segments.text: How do you mean you're the mediator?

segments.speaker: Boy
segments.text: I'm actually not sure what mediator means. I just felt like saying it. I think it means a guy who keeps peace. Like, keeping them from killing each other.

segments.speaker: Reporter
segments.text: They can use a guy like you in the Middle East maybe.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: One of the little brothers signals for the microphone.

segments.speaker: Little Brother
segments.text: Get it? Middle East. Because he's in the middle, and he's out east. Get it? Middle East.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: There's nothing particularly notable about this rest stop. It's one of thousands all over the country, the kind of place we'd stop for 10 minutes on a holiday weekend, run inside, use the restroom, buy a burger or a coffee, head back out on the road.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But if you stayed for more than 10 minutes, you might end up talking to one of these kids or to one of the couples who are dropping off children at college, like this reporter did.

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: --the last kid off to school, so now we're the new empty nesters right now.

segments.speaker: Reporter
segments.text: I know. How do you feel about that?

segments.speaker: Mom
segments.text: I'm cooking things that I've never tried.

segments.speaker: Dad
segments.text: Yeah, and I'm eating things that I've never tried.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: There's some folks on the way back from a family reunion, might complain about the traffic.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: And suddenly a clown truck filled with clowns cut us off.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Or there's this guy, whose entertainment on his weekly four-hour drive isn't the radio or the CD player.

segments.speaker: Driver
segments.text: Well, truthfully, so none of the police folk out there are listening, I usually read the newspaper on the way up, or a book.

segments.speaker: Reporter
segments.text: Are you kidding me?

segments.speaker: Driver
segments.text: Here and there on the way up.

segments.speaker: Reporter
segments.text: And you've been doing it for six or seven years, and you've not had an accident?

segments.speaker: Driver
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Reporter
segments.text: That seems to me to be pure luck.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: There's a family driving six hours to visit their dad in prison; a young couple looking for a place to have their wedding; two brothers on the way to compete in the rodeo; a 16-year-old standing inside the rest stop nursing a tea, taking a break from her own family. She's on an eight-hour car trip with her dad, her grandma, her sister, and a couple of brothers. She explains to a reporter.

segments.speaker: Girl
segments.text: Well, it's very noisy, you could say that. Because everybody's arguing or talking about sports. We were just having an argument on who's better, Muhammad Ali or Mike Tyson? And Mike Tyson won. So my dad nearly stopped the car to argue and say, no, Mike Tyson is better. So it was just very hectic.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Coincidentally, a little later, Mike Tyson's name comes up again, in conversation with the prep cook named Ozzy, who works at the rest stop.

segments.speaker: Ozzy
segments.text: Sometimes I see movie stars. I see Tyson in person.

segments.speaker: Reporter
segments.text: Mike Tyson.

segments.speaker: Ozzy
segments.text: Mike Tyson was here. He has a tiny voice. How are you doing, man? Can I get ice cream? You know? So I see Mario Cuomo. I see this old lady who got a lot of plastic surgeries.

segments.speaker: Reporter
segments.text: Joan Rivers.

segments.speaker: Ozzy
segments.text: Yes, she was here, too.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Poor Joan Rivers. The two strangers can get her name across simply by saying, "the old lady who got a lot of plastic surgery."

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Nine of us came to this rest stop with tape recorders on a weekend in the middle of August, all the way back in 2009. Today's show is a rerun. It was two weeks before Labor Day, the time of year when over 10,000 people pass through this rest stop each day. We thought that, for once, we would not leave after just 10 minutes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Stick around and find out who all these people are, where they're going, what they're thinking about. We found love stories, and hardcore partiers, and inexplicably angry people, and all kinds of others. We bring you those stories in this special hour of our show for this holiday weekend when so many of us are on the road. WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The name of this particular rest stop is the Plattekill Travel Plaza. It's on the New York Thruway, I-87, about an hour and a half north of New York City on the northbound side of the highway. It's shiny and recently renovated with five restaurants in the food court-- Nathan's Hot Dog, Arthur Treacher's Fish and Chips, Roy Rogers, a Canadian sandwich shop called Brioche Duree, and a Starbucks-- plus a travel mart that sells sodas, and chips and gum, and stuff like that.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: All these concessions and the cleaning crews and everything else are run by a company called HMS Host, which does this kind of thing in airports and travel plazas across the country. They have 120 employees here, and a half dozen managers, and a general manager.

segments.speaker: Robert Woodill
segments.text: I think we have a very strong weekend as we get into the end of summer.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This is the general manager, Robert Woodill, a friendly, upbeat guy who carries a folded piece of paper that he pulls out and unfolds and refers to constantly through the day, which has a list of sales figures for every half hour of the day.

segments.speaker: Robert Woodill
segments.text: All it simply is, is it's my half hour reports of last year on this day, so I can compare my sales the last year and see where we're at. And we do it usually at, like, 11 o'clock, and then every hour or so, we take a quick reading just to see where we're at.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And explain when is the crazy time.

segments.speaker: Robert Woodill
segments.text: Today, it'll be probably from, like, 12 o'clock till 7 o'clock, very solid and steady. And then tomorrow morning, it'll pick up again. And I think as we're getting to the end of summer, there's a big race in Saratoga this week. People have booked their rooms for Lake George, and it's the end of summer. People want to go and go on vacation. So I think we're going to have a good weekend.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We did our taping on Friday and Saturday, two weeks before Labor Day, because those are the biggest days and the biggest month here. In August, the rest stop makes a fourth of its money for the whole year. And it's crucial that Robert makes his goals this weekend because it's built into the rest stop business that there are a couple months every year when he just breaks even or loses money.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Also, he wants to do better than his rival-- his rival, a rest stop in Maine, run by a guy named Andy Tucci.

segments.speaker: Robert Woodill
segments.text: Kennebunk North, usually, and I are neck and neck. And we never place any wagers, but you know, they're Red Sox fans, we're Yankee fans. And we go back and forth on that, as well as discussing who's going to have the record sales for the day.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Who won last weekend?

segments.speaker: Robert Woodill
segments.text: Andy. Andy beat me red like a lobster, if you want. That's what I told him. He beat me both days, but I think I'm going to get it back this weekend, so. I hope this week, the Yankees sweep the Red Sox, and then he'll be really quiet.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Robert was fully staffed for the rush. He had his best cashiers on. And now, he just needed the crowds, the big summer weekend crowds.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: We chose this particular rest stop because, a couple years ago, I came here on the way to a wedding, and I noticed that a couple of the college students working at the Starbucks were speaking Polish. When I asked, they said, yeah, they were from Poland, here for the summer, on a special visa program called the J-1 program, where they live in the United States and work for three months at the rest stop and then get to travel for a month in America before flying home.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And it seemed like such a crazy thing to fly all the way to America and then be stuck behind a counter in the middle of nowhere for the summer. I wondered if they felt cheated. I wanted to come back and find out.

segments.speaker: Sandy
segments.text: I'm Sandy, and I'm from Taiwan. And I work at Starbucks in Plattekill Travel Plaza.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: There are no Polish students this summer. It's mostly Taiwanese and Ukrainians working in Plattekill. Sandy's name back home is Moche Cho. She's a college junior and English major. This is her second year doing this summer work program. Last year, she was one of hundreds of foreign students who got jobs at Cedar Point Amusement Park in Sandusky, Ohio.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But this year, she wanted to see a different part of the country and signed up for this location because of two magic words-- New York.

segments.speaker: Sandy
segments.text: I love New York. Last year, I went to New York City just three days. So this time, I want to stay in New York City more.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then when you got here, were you surprised how far it was from New York City?

segments.speaker: Sandy
segments.text: Yes, very surprised. Yeah. So actually, I'm a little regret about I choose this place, yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: She knew the rest stop wasn't in New York City. She just thought it would be a little closer and easier to get to. Without a car, everything's a hassle. So she hasn't seen New York at all this summer. The only place she's gone is some outlet stores. When she's not at work, she hangs around the apartment with five other students, all women who came over from Asia this summer to work at the rest stop.

segments.speaker: Sandy
segments.text: When we have day off, we will go to a supermarket to buy grocery. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That's it?

segments.speaker: Sandy
segments.text: Maybe go to a restaurant to eat something.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What's the best thing that's happened this summer on your trip?

segments.speaker: Sandy
segments.text: This summer? So far, I didn't make happiness in this trip. So far, no.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wait, you haven't had much that's been so good this trip?

segments.speaker: Sandy
segments.text: No, so far.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So this seemed, frankly, a little sad. A bunch of students quietly tolerating their summers, counting the days until they could finally travel the country. Cooking food they don't eat, like hamburgers, and drinks they'd never heard of before arriving here, like frappucinos, all for people who have cars at a place that's all about cars on the side of the highway, but without cars of their own. I felt bad for them.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And then I started talking to the Ukrainian students.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And how's it going?

segments.speaker: Evgenia Trekasa
segments.text: Very good. I think that I really get a very big, huge experience here because I like this place, and I want to come back here. It's really true. I'm happy that I'm here.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Evgenia Trekasa goes by the name Jane or Angelina here in the States. She's 18, entering her junior year of college. It's her first time away so long from her parents, and she misses them terribly, but it's also very exciting. She says that in the first week or two in Plattekill, she and the other Ukrainians felt stranded, same as the girls from Taiwan and Hong Kong felt.

segments.speaker: Evgenia Trekasa
segments.text: Because that we don't have a car, we can't drive. We just can take a bus, so that's why. But then we find friends that, like, when we have a day off, they always can take us. Like, all the guys, it's OK. We will show you beautiful places. So when we have a day off, we always go to somewhere. We never stay at home.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What happened is that the Ukrainians befriended a couple of the American teenagers who work at the rest stop, and those teenagers introduced them to other young people. And before they knew it, they had rides to the mall, to Six Flags Amusement Park, to New York City.

segments.speaker: Adelaide Giron
segments.text: My name is Adelaide Giron. I'm 19. I work at Roy Rogers.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Adelaide is a big, cheerful, fun-loving guy and probably the American who's gotten closest to the Ukrainians. In two years working at the Roy Rogers at the rest stop, he's seen lots of foreign students come through.

segments.speaker: Adelaide Giron
segments.text: I think this group has definitely, by far, been my favorite.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Why?

segments.speaker: Adelaide Giron
segments.text: I felt like the other groups before, I've gotten attached to them. But this group, I think it's since I'm in college and they're in college. And we drink, and I drink, and they drink. And it's a fun experience.

segments.speaker: Adelaide Giron
segments.text: I just recently got my license about two years ago-- actually, a year and a half ago. Before that, I was driving illegally, so I really couldn't drive all over the place. But now that I got my license, so, like, [BLEEP] I'm driving everywhere.

segments.speaker: Adelaide Giron
segments.text: So I hang out with them. I take them shopping. At night, we go, like, swimming at this lake, trespassing. Who cares, though? Just having a good time. We're young. The cops showed up one time. We had alcohol on us. It was a pretty bad story.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: For a while, he says he was going over to their apartment three times a week-- Fridays, Saturdays, and Wednesdays for parties-- parties he taught them how to throw. Here's one of his students in this matter, Peter Molov, one of the Ukrainians.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What's your favorite thing that you've done so far since you've been here?

segments.speaker: Peter Molov
segments.text: Favorite thing? Probably the parties. Parties. They're a lot different than in our country. If we want to have parties, we just go to the club in our country, in Ukraine. Go to the club, loud music and stuff, you know.

segments.speaker: Peter Molov
segments.text: But since we came here, we get to know other Americans, and they said, let's have a party. Well, OK, let's go to the club. Why to the club? Let's do it at home. OK. We go to home. They showed us games they play.

segments.speaker: Adelaide Giron
segments.text: Beer pong. Introduced them to my beer funnel-- they'd never seen that before. We showed them flip cup. We showed them how to play flip cup, and--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I don't even know what that is.

segments.speaker: Adelaide Giron
segments.text: Really? It's a good buzz-getter.

segments.speaker: Peter Molov
segments.text: It is fun. A lot of people play, so it's really fun.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And you didn't have beer pong back in Ukraine?

segments.speaker: Peter Molov
segments.text: No. I never knew.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Will you be taking that back to show your friends back home?

segments.speaker: Peter Molov
segments.text: Oh, yeah. We even want to buy a beer pong table, you know? Special for it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I'm not sure they call it a beer pong table.

segments.speaker: Adelaide Giron
segments.text: They're pretty good for not knowing what beer pong is. Like, we just introduced them to beer pong two months ago, and yet, they're better than me. So yeah, we actually have, like, tournaments going on sometimes, and the Ukrainians end up on top most of the time. So yeah.

segments.speaker: Dasha
segments.text: It's impossible to drink so much as Americans do. Americans really drink very much.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: This is Dasha, another 19-year-old from Ukraine. She said most of the parties here in America in their apartment or out by the lake went until dawn.

segments.speaker: Dasha
segments.text: At 6:00 AM, 7:00 AM. And then the most fun is then when you work from 9:00 AM and you don't sleep at all. Like, one day, I just slept 30 minutes. I woke up and went to work.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: That was the most fun?

segments.speaker: Dasha
segments.text: Yeah. As for me, I was dying at work.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Fortunately, she works at a Starbucks. The Plattekill Rest Stop has employed foreign students for nearly a decade. They're hard workers and easier to schedule into shifts than American teenagers, who are always needing time off for family vacations, and sports practice, and other activities. There's a group in the summer and then smaller groups in the winter and spring.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And the Plattekill Rest Stop is a close knit enough place that people cry when they leave. One of the managers told me how she still emails kids from Brazil and Peru who worked here years ago. At least one marriage has come out of this, between an American worker and a Bulgarian girl.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Though all the managers of the rest stop agreed that they like the Ukrainians, they're good kids, but the Ukrainians are the rowdiest group with the most issues they have ever had, hands down. Probably because the Ukrainians are the first group that were friends back in their home country. They came to Plattekill for a summer adventure.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: They're having too much fun, one manager told me. Fireworks after 2:00 AM, complaints from neighbors. The police have come out a few times, because of the noise. Robert, the general manager, has no idea where he's going to find them housing if their landlord evicts them.

segments.speaker: Robert Woodill
segments.text: It's been a little bit of a rough summer with them. They're enjoying it. They're college kids. And I think the thing is they forget that they're not living in the dorms. They live in an apartment complex, where there's families, and kids, and little kids. So they just have to be more respectful at times.

segments.speaker: Robert Woodill
segments.text: It's not like we don't want them have a good time. You got to make sure you draw the line someplace and say, OK, maybe 1 o'clock is late enough. Or the people are going to work because it's a Tuesday, and you just got to kind of be good neighbors.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: As it turned out, everything came to a head the night before we arrived to record with an all-night party that Adelaide says was their craziest ever-- a party that was not thrown by the Ukrainians. It was the very first party thrown by the girls from Taiwan, total turnaround for them. Adelaide says before this, he and the Ukrainians had only invited them to one party.

segments.speaker: Adelaide Giron
segments.text: And they really don't drink, so they got drunk off a couple of beers. And we just-- they couldn't hang, so we just didn't invite them anymore.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But now they threw this party, a goodbye party for one of the girls who was leaving early, and they partied with the best of them, everybody dancing and making noise. After the second beer run, there was a late night beer fight with people pouring their drinks on each other. As usual, all this bothering the neighbors.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Then what was it, they complained to the landlord?

segments.speaker: Adelaide Giron
segments.text: Yeah. The landlord doesn't like me or my other friends hanging around there. He actually refers to me as a big crazy Mexican that walks around, but. So I don't know. I don't think I'm a big crazy Mexican at all. I'm a gentle giant, really.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And so then Robert had a talk with everybody?

segments.speaker: Adelaide Giron
segments.text: Yeah. He had a talk with everybody.

segments.speaker: Robert Woodill
segments.text: And it was kind of time to play the heavy-handed dad and just to make sure that they get the full message that this can't go on.

segments.speaker: Dasha
segments.text: That we shouldn't have any more parties here. We should be quiet because if there will be one more party, they will send us home. They will, like, break our contract with Plaza, and then there will be no more students in Plaza the next year.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And what do you think of that?

segments.speaker: Dasha
segments.text: I don't know. Just, I don't really care they will have any other students next summer. Because I won't be there.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: The American kids also got a warning from their boss. Again, here's Adelaide.

segments.speaker: Adelaide Giron
segments.text: You know, just to stop going over there. The landlord doesn't want me on his property. He sees me or my car, it's getting towed at my expense. I'm going to get charged for trespassing.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And so what are you going to do?

segments.speaker: Adelaide Giron
segments.text: Well, I'll probably still go over. [BLEEP] it. There's really nothing-- I mean, if they say anything, I'll just be like, oh, OK. It won't happen again, officer. And of course it'll happen again, but.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And do you worry that you could get the Ukrainians in trouble in a way that they'd get sent back early?

segments.speaker: Adelaide Giron
segments.text: I hope not, but if they do, it's all a good time. And I told them if anything happens, I'm deeply sorry, but whatever happens happens. There's nothing we can do.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And that, everybody says, was the last big party of the year. But no matter. It was still a great summer. I asked Evgenia if she ever felt jealous of all the travelers she saw pass through the rest stop, people on the way to vacations while she was stuck working. And she said never. She'd come so far to get here.

segments.speaker: Evgenia Trekasa
segments.text: They should be jealous of me, because I'm here.

segments.speaker: Lisa Pollak
segments.text: Inside the rest stop, right when you enter the lobby, between the bathroom and the food court, is this room full of racks of brochures.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Lisa Pollak is one of the gang of nine reporters that we had at Plattekill.

segments.speaker: Lisa Pollak
segments.text: You know those brochures you'll see in the lobby of a discount hotel, the ones advertising local attractions that inevitably, no matter where in the country you are, include a water park and an underground cavern tour? It's that, floor to ceiling.

segments.speaker: Lisa Pollak
segments.text: This is the New York State Information Center. It confusingly is run not by New York State, but by a private company that charges businesses to display their pamphlets here. The manager of the center is a guy named Lenny Wheat. He also stands behind a counter offering travel advice to the lost.

segments.speaker: Lisa Pollak
segments.text: When I talk to Lenny, he gets this look on his face, almost like he feels a little sorry for me. Because I think I'm in the middle of nowhere, and he thinks I have no idea what I'm missing.

segments.speaker: Lenny Wheat
segments.text: Right here, the next exit alone, you have best rock climbing in the country here.

segments.speaker: Lisa Pollak
segments.text: Oh, seriously?

segments.speaker: Lenny Wheat
segments.text: Yeah. It's the Napa Valley of the east around here. We have the oldest vineyards, the oldest winery, one of the best wineries. You have the best hotel resort spa in the United States in the area here, too.

segments.speaker: Lisa Pollak
segments.text: Wait, how do you know it's the best in the--

segments.speaker: Lenny Wheat
segments.text: That's according to Mobil Travel Guide and Day Spa Magazine. I got one of the best dude ranches in the country up here by New Paltz, too.

segments.speaker: Lisa Pollak
segments.text: No, you don't.

segments.speaker: Lenny Wheat
segments.text: Yes, Rocking Horse Ranch Resort. Yeah, great place to take a family.

segments.speaker: Lisa Pollak
segments.text: By the time Lenny tells me about something called the Catamount Adventure Park-- largest adventure park in North America, according to the brochure--

segments.speaker: Lenny Wheat
segments.text: There's 120 things to do there.

segments.speaker: Lisa Pollak
segments.text: --I am so overwhelmed by superlatives that I just take his word for it. Lenny knows this area. He's a local, lives eight minutes away. And he used to drive for a messenger service so he's an expert at getting directions. I found it especially impressive when he told travelers the exact number of miles between highway exits by memory.

segments.speaker: Lisa Pollak
segments.text: But Lenny actually ended up in this job by accident. His neighbor used to work here, and Lenny would visit him from time to time to help out.

segments.speaker: Lenny Wheat
segments.text: And he was feeling ill one day, and I was like-- he says, you think you can stay here and do this? And I'm like, sure, why not? I mean, I know my way around. I know the roads, so. And he had some issues and stuff, diabetes and stuff, and wound up taking time out and stuff. He recently passed away and stuff.

segments.speaker: Lisa Pollak
segments.text: I'm so sorry.

segments.speaker: Lenny Wheat
segments.text: So but kind of like sometimes you feel like what you've done in your life is-- and it comes together, that it's like you were meant to do something, you know?

segments.speaker: Lisa Pollak
segments.text: So you're saying it kind of seemed like it was meant to be?

segments.speaker: Lenny Wheat
segments.text: Sometimes it feels that way.

segments.speaker: Lisa Pollak
segments.text: I hung out with Lenny for a couple hours. I saw him cheerfully field dozens of information requests, everything from where to buy beer-- nowhere at the rest stop, but try New Paltz, there's a lot of college kids there-- to how to get to Maryland. A crucial first step-- turn around. Maryland is south of here. You are headed north.

segments.speaker: Lisa Pollak
segments.text: When anyone wanders in to browse, Lenny pounces.

segments.speaker: Lenny Wheat
segments.text: What's your destination of today?

segments.speaker: Lisa Pollak
segments.text: Lake George, the guy says.

segments.speaker: Lenny Wheat
segments.text: OK. Can I get you anything for Lake George? We just got in the fall events guide, too.

segments.speaker: Tourist
segments.text: Sure, if you want to.

segments.speaker: Lenny Wheat
segments.text: Anything for Washington County on the other side of the lake? Anything on hiking?

segments.speaker: Tourist
segments.text: No.

segments.speaker: Lenny Wheat
segments.text: Waterways? Whitewater rafting?

segments.speaker: Tourist
segments.text: Waterways.

segments.speaker: Lenny Wheat
segments.text: Waterways, OK.

segments.speaker: Lisa Pollak

segments.text: Yeah, not the direction. The direction thing has to be down pat. I lost control.

segments.speaker: Debbie Longo
segments.text: I really hate my whole family right now. They didn't want to leave in the morning. God forbid we leave in the morning.

segments.speaker: Jay Allison
segments.text: Next time you'll leave in the morning.

segments.speaker: Tony Longo
segments.text: Oh, we'll leave in the morning next time.

segments.speaker: Debbie Longo
segments.text: Next time, I'm not coming.

segments.speaker: Jay Allison
segments.text: It's after 3:00 in the morning, and they've been lost for hours. And Debbie Longo says she's not a happy camper. But you can tell she is.

segments.speaker: Debbie Longo
segments.text: There's no soft serve, and it's not taking my money. I don't care anymore. I don't care. I'm going to get fat, and I don't care. I'm going to blow up like a balloon. And you're going to have a big fat wife.

segments.speaker: Tony Longo
segments.text: That's OK.

segments.speaker: Debbie Longo
segments.text: OK.

segments.speaker: Tony Longo
segments.text: But we stay happy.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Isn't there some truism about if you want to test your relationship, go on a long drive together? What I'm saying is, I'm expecting a lot of grouchiness here at the rest stop during the graveyard shift-- scowls, sniping, mutual recrimination.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Instead, I keep seeing couple after couple walk up to the glass doors of the rest stop and reach for each other's hands right before they walk through. Instinctively, like, here we go, you and me. Couples of every age-- 20s, 40s, 60s.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: What are your names?

segments.speaker: Edetta
segments.text: Edetta.

segments.speaker: Peter
segments.text: And I'm Peter.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Edetta and Peter are on a five-hour drive to pick up their kids from summer camp, their first time at camp. In other words, a Parenting 101 trip-- unexciting, long, and happening at an inconvenient time. But listen to them laughing.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Did the kids want to go, or did you say, "You're going?"

segments.speaker: Peter
segments.text: We kind of made them go.

segments.speaker: Peter
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Edetta
segments.text: And our oldest left for college exactly for the same time, so it works well.

segments.speaker: Peter
segments.text: Free time for ourselves, and they have free time for themselves.

segments.speaker: Peter
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: It's at this point that I blurt out the most obvious and inappropriate question.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: What did you do with your free time?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Which they handle admirably.

segments.speaker: Edetta
segments.text: We really had time to connect.

segments.speaker: Peter
segments.text: Had some romantic dinners and spend time together.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: When was the last time you had time to do that before this?

segments.speaker: Peter
segments.text: Oh, 20 years ago.

segments.speaker: Peter
segments.text: [LAUGHTER]

segments.speaker: Edetta
segments.text: Oh, I remember back then.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: And there's more giddiness inside the rest stop. Another couple, Lisa and Marcus.

segments.speaker: Lisa
segments.text: Did you see me giving him little kisses and telling him how cute he was when he walked in?

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Lisa and Marcus, as you can tell, are in deep. They're looking at a map on the wall of this half-closed rest stop on their way up to Lake Champlain to go camping. It's the middle of the night. They've gotten lost already, not sure where they're going to sleep. But the two of them cannot stop smiling. I can feel endorphins radiating from them in waves. They met salsa dancing less than a year ago, and love is making them ambitious.

segments.speaker: Lisa
segments.text: We're planning on maybe moving to Argentina.

segments.speaker: Marcus
segments.text: And we started already dancing tango here in Philadelphia. So we want to become professional tango dancers. No, that's a joke.

segments.speaker: Lisa
segments.text: No, it's not.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Outside the rest stop, Katarina and Johnny are sitting next to each other on a bench. Not a bench in a beautiful park, a bench looking out on a highway and a parking lot. Of course they don't care. In fact, they seem not to have noticed at all.

segments.speaker: Katarina
segments.text: We're going to Montreal, Canada.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: You're going to Montreal?

segments.speaker: Katarina
segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Johnny
segments.text: Yeah, we're coming from New York, and we're going to Montreal.

segments.speaker: Katarina
segments.text: Right, yeah.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: Johnny is finishing up his residency, but he's not sure he even wants to be a doctor. 35 years old with more than $200,000 in school debt. But he doesn't want to talk about that. He's on a road trip with his girl. He brushes off my questions, leans into the microphone, and steers us back to what we should be talking about.

segments.speaker: Johnny
segments.text: (SINGING) Love me tender, love me true, never let me go. Oh my god.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: But even at a rest stop that's fizzy with love, there is heartache. As I'm standing outside, a man asks what I'm doing. So I ask what he's doing. We end up talking for a while. His name is Dan. He's driving back to upstate New York after a day in New York City.

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: Spent some time with my boys.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: How old are they?

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: 19 and 20-- oh my god-- 23.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: How often do you see them?

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: Not often enough. I'm trying to make it more regular 'cause I just got divorced, like, a year or so ago, and so. They're staying with their mom, so I'm seeing less of them. Try to get to see them, like, once a month.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: How is the divorce for them?

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: I don't really know. It seems to be OK for them, you know? It's a little weird still, but we still try to do things together and--

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: You and your ex-wife and the kids?

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: No, I don't do things with her anymore. Last year, my son's 18th birthday, we went skydiving together.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: All four of you.

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: Yeah, all four of us. Like, she wanted her boyfriend to come. And I was like-- I actually called him and said, don't come.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: You called him?

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: Yeah. I called him, left him a message. It was a very polite message. And I was like, Michael, please don't come.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: You know him. You have his number.

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: Yeah. I knew him, yeah. So. It was a tough thing. She wanted him to come and, like, go on my son's 18th birthday. And it was like, really, it was just too weird. It's a very weird thing, trying to be friends with your ex, and then you can't really be friends. And then you have this other girlfriend, and then it's just like it's such a difficult thing.

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: She didn't want me to go to the house to pick the boys up. And then one week, we're having a good conversation, and next week, something like that comes up. And you're like-- you have the thing. You want to call that person, and yell at them, and talk to them about it. But you don't have that relationship anymore.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: That's a hard moment, when you realize, right, we don't have that relationship anymore.

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: Try to go to counseling and stuff and try to get her to come back.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: She didn't want to go to counseling?

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: She went with me one time, but then she wouldn't stop seeing this guy, this other guy she was seeing. So I mean, that kind of-- I made her pay the copay and we left.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: This other guy, Michael.

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: Yeah. I had actually met him. I had met him at a party and her and him had become friends. And they just became more and more intimate. And instead of trying to work stuff out with me, she was trying to work stuff out with him, so-- I just think about it a lot. I beat myself up for where did I go wrong as a father, as a husband or whatever. And I'm basically 45 years old, and I figure half my life is over. And I'm really trying to figure out what to do with the next half.

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: I know this is just a rest stop, but really, some kind of love force field is in effect here tonight. Because guess what? Dan has a new girlfriend. She's at the rest stop with him, just doesn't want to talk into a microphone. They met through a singles group, and they've been together long enough that they've started meeting each other's kids. It's still complicated, but wow, it feels great.

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: I just told her tonight. I said I don't know what I would do with somebody else in my life. I mean, this is-- I found a woman that really loves me. And I'm, like, so over bowled by that, you know? It's just, it's--

segments.speaker: Nancy Updike
segments.text: It's like a miracle.

segments.speaker: Dan
segments.text: Yeah, it is. I'm optimistic about the future. Very optimistic.

segments.speaker: Jay Allison
segments.text: In the parking lot, when I first saw Stevie G from a distance, I thought he was naked.

segments.speaker: Stevie G
segments.text: And right now, I'm de-kinking the muscles in my buttock.

segments.speaker: Jay Allison
segments.text: Then he kicked one leg in the air above his head, and I saw he was wearing little white gym shoes.

segments.speaker: Stevie G
segments.text: Oh, it opens up the Fountain of Youth in the front of the hip joint.

segments.speaker: Jay Allison
segments.text: And then he jumped into a pool of light, and I saw he actually had on some tiny black nylon shorts. Stevie G teaches bodywork, pilates, yoga, massage, and such. And he stopped at this rest stop to stretch and move. It's hard not to notice, though, that while Stevie is working out in the parking lot, he's simultaneously smoking a hand-rolled cigarette.

segments.speaker: Stevie G
segments.text: That's what I am, you know? Unfortunately, I'm polluting my lungs, but they're doing well. I clean them out on a daily basis.

segments.speaker: Jay Allison
segments.text: How do you clean them out?

segments.speaker: Stevie G
segments.text: Usually a mixture of running, and steaming, and meditational breathing, and not swallowing what I cough up. I always spit it out. Like, I have a little cup. I can spit out all-- I don't never swallow it.

segments.speaker: Jay Allison
segments.text: Our conversation, by the way, is happening next to Stevie's vehicle, which figures largely in his life. It's an old yellow school bus he got up in Woodstock to start a volunteer service program.

segments.speaker: Stevie G
segments.text: Picking up the drunk people, like, going into the bars and finding the ones and say, all right, who looks really bombed? Offer them a free ride home.

segments.speaker: Jay Allison
segments.text: But now Stevie G has a larger vision for the bus. He wants to build a health center made of school buses. Before he leaves the rest stop, Stevie G gets out a big foam roller and takes it to his favorite spot for a final stretch.

segments.speaker: Stevie G
segments.text: All right, we got all the big 18 wheeler trucks on one side. We've got all the smaller cars over here on the other. We are on 87 highway. This is where I think it's the cleanest. You just got to watch out to see if the dogs have been here.

segments.speaker: Stevie G
segments.text: Abracadabra, scoop that belly, burn the jelly, America. You gotta get off your fat one and do something good, something good like the solid oak wood. Get out there and help others. And especially help yourself to be your best, so that you are not a cranky old fool. Now we all got to pull up the hill.

segments.speaker: Jay Allison
segments.text: Stevie rolls all around the sidewalk, with truckers looking down at him from their cabs. He doesn't notice. When he's all loosened up, he picks up his roller and heads back to his vehicle.

segments.speaker: Jay Allison
segments.text: [ENGINE STARTING]

segments.speaker: Stevie G
segments.text: Oh, it sounds good. That's my baby. Take care. Take it easy.

segments.speaker: Jay Allison
segments.text: Stevie G coughs up some phlegm, spits it out, and heads off for Woodstock.

segments.speaker: Jay Allison
segments.text: It's morning. English sparrows are congregating like crazy in the trees just outside the rest stop doors. Standing out in the parking lot, nine-year-old Brian Belco looks kind of like a bird, actually. His eyes are bright. His arms are stiff at his sides and held out a bit like wings. And when he speaks into the microphone, he bobs his head forward, like he's pecking at it.

segments.speaker: Brian Belco
segments.text: We're going fishing up in Swanton's Mine.

segments.speaker: Jay Allison
segments.text: Yeah, what are you going to catch?

segments.speaker: Brian Belco
segments.text: Bass, pike, pickerel, perch.

segments.speaker: Jay Allison
segments.text: Wow, it sounds like you've done this before.

segments.speaker: Brian Belco
segments.text: Yep. But the tradition started with my family. It started with my great grandfather.

segments.speaker: Jay Allison
segments.text: Is that right?

segments.speaker: Brian Belco
segments.text: My great grandfather was a great fisherman. He really liked fishing, so he went up to Lake Champlain. And some of the cabins were built right over the historic battlefield of the war in 1842, the Battle of Lake Champlain.

segments.speaker: Jay Allison
segments.text: You're a student.

segments.speaker: Brian Belco
segments.text: This is my first radio interview ever.

segments.speaker: Jay Allison
segments.text: Really?

segments.speaker: Brian Belco
segments.text: Yep.

segments.speaker: Jay Allison
segments.text: You did great.

segments.speaker: Brian Belco
segments.text: I know. I'm really, really excited.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Say goodbye.

segments.speaker: Brian Belco
segments.text: Bye.

segments.speaker: Jay Allison
segments.text: Bye. Have a great vacation.

segments.speaker: Man
segments.text: Thanks.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And with the new day here, we have just the time for one final note before we go. Final tallies from the battle between the rest stops in Plattekill and Maine. At the end of the afternoon, after our two days in Plattekill, I can report to you that business never really picked up for either rest stop. And after two days on Saturday afternoon, Robert told me he only had one consolation for the weekend-- he beat Andy.

segments.speaker: Robert Woodill
segments.text: I'm the king for the day. I beat Andy, and the Red Sox got smacked around and massacred by the Yankees. The unfortunate thing is being king for the day when you miss your sales by seven grand isn't so good. And everybody was down. So it was a bad day for everybody. Maine-- Andy sent out a quick note, not hitting his numbers at all.

segments.speaker: Robert Woodill
segments.text: But you know, we're ready for next weekend. We still got two more weekends to go. I still think they're coming. I mean, yeah, in this business, you've got to be positive.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When I left, he was around $12,000 down for two days, 7% or 8% lower than where he needed to be. But all this rain, he said, could make for really beautiful leaves upstate come the fall. A lot of people could get on the roads for that to look at those leaves. He could still turn this around.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Today's show was reported in 2009. In the years since, Robert, the general manager, has been promoted several times. He's now a senior director of Motorways, overseeing travel plazas in the New York Thruway, the main turnpike, and a few Starbucks in Massachusetts-- which means, of course, that the competition between Plattekill and Andy in Kennebunkport came to an end. Though, Robert says, they do still argue about baseball.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: You can still find Lenny Wheat dispensing travel advice and Clara Dragon behind the register at Plattekill, though they've stopped using J-1 visas to bring in foreign students.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Well, our program was produced today by Sean Cole and myself, with Alex Blumberg, Jane Marie, Sarah Koenig, Lisa Pollak, Alyssa Shipp, and Nancy Updike. segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Thanks, as always, to our program's co-founder, Mr. Torey Malatia, who says do not believe his reputation. Do not believe what people say about him. It's not true.

segments.speaker: Adelaide Giron
segments.text: I don't think I'm a big crazy Mexican at all. I'm a gentle giant, really.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: I'm Ira Glass. Back next week with more stories of This American Life.
